The Fluorescent Library of Lost Thoughts

In the quiet hours of dawn, when the city is still and the only sound is the hum of electricity, I often find myself wandering the deserted aisles of my mind. It's a labyrinthine place, full of twisting corridors and narrow staircases that lead to nowhere, but I always seem to find my way back to the starting point. And it's in this fluorescent-lit library of lost thoughts that I spend most of my waking hours, searching for the forgotten stories of my past.

I remember the smell of old books and the texture of worn pages, the way my fingers would tremble as I turned the leaves and the words began to bleed from the ink. It was as if the stories themselves were alive, whispering secrets to each other when no one was around. My mother, a scholar of dusty tomes, would take me on these midnight excursions, and I'd sit beside her, awestruck, as she poured over ancient texts. She'd tell me tales of lost civilizations, of phantoms who walked the earth, of miracles that defied explanation. And I, entranced, would absorb it all, filing it away in this library of dreams.

But the truth is, most of what I know was never even mine to begin with. I've lived so many lives, worn so many masks, that I've lost track of who I am. My name is like a refrain, echoing through the chambers of my mind, a reminder that even identity is a myth, a fragile construct that can be stripped away in an instant. I've been a world traveler, a poet, a spy, a politician – and yet, not one of these selves feels quite real. I'm searching for a story that's mine alone, something that doesn't belong to anyone else, but the more I try to hold on to it, the more it slips through my fingers.

One day, I stumbled upon an old chalkboard in a room that seemed to belong to no one. It was covered in cryptic symbols, like mixtures of code and art. The letters danced, seemingly alive, and I became obsessed with deciphering them. I think it was because they didn't belong to anyone; they were oracles of mystery, speaking in tongues that only the initiated could understand. I'd stare at those symbols for hours, mesmerized by the shapes, the eternities, and the geometric tendrils that seemed to intersect in impossible ways. Was I trying to find the secret language, the code that unlocked all the hidden doors of the universe? Or was it just a distraction from the scraps of my own memories?

Rest is also a subject, one I've wrestled with for what feels like an eternity. Not just sleep, but the kind that happens when you're underwater, trapped in a seemingly bottomless expanse of nothing, swaying like a leaf on a breeze that has no known source. The way I become lost in abandon, just letting go, until I'm back on the surface, gasping for air, shattered by the realization that I'm awake, that everything is real. And the search for rest becomes a searching of self, dialectics of disrupting all redundancy in becoming.
